issues.what: The interval from 40 to 50 years is labeled “gap: no data,” but its count is 2.
issues.why: A gap requires no observed data in the interval. All six bins have positive counts, so the parameters do not show the gap asserted by the title, subtitle, note, and alt text.

issues.what: The alt text states there are 38 customers and gives the fourth bin a count of 0.
issues.why: The actual counts are 7, 14, 9, 2, 5, and 3, totaling 40 customers.

issues.what: The count for the bin from 40 to 50 is 2 in the drawing parameters, but the alt text and label claim it has 0 observations (a gap).
issues.why: The figure will display a bar of height 2 in the 40-50 interval, contradicting the claim that this interval is a gap with no observed data.

issues.what: The note and alt text incorrectly define the gap as the interval with the most observations and identify the tallest bar, ages 20–30, as the gap.
issues.why: A gap contains no observed data. The counts show the gap at ages 40–50, with 0 customers; ages 20–30 has 14 customers and is the modal bin, not a gap.

issues.what: The measure label reads "gap: most data."
issues.why: This contradicts the definition of a gap as a region with no observed data, regardless of which bin the label marks.

issues.what: The subtitle, note, alt text, and measure label define a 'gap' as the interval with the most observations (the tallest bar).
issues.why: A gap is a region in a distribution with no observed data (count of 0). Defining it as the interval with the most observations is factually incorrect and contradicts the authored reference entry's claim.

issues.what: The alt text identifies the bin from 20 to 30 years (height 14) as the gap.
issues.why: The bin with 0 observations is from 40 to 50 years. The bin from 20 to 30 years is the peak (mode) of the distribution, not a gap.

issues.what: The plotted relative frequencies are assigned to the opposite classes from those described in the alt text.
issues.why: The parameters assign Class A 40% Walk, 8% Bike, 12% Bus, and 40% Car, and Class B 20%, 10%, 30%, and 40%, respectively. The alt text reverses these assignments.

issues.what: The plotted relative frequencies are incompatible with the labelled class sizes.
issues.why: For Class A's 40 students, 8% biking and 12% taking the bus imply 3.2 and 4.8 students. For Class B's 25 students, 10% biking and 30% taking the bus imply 2.5 and 7.5 students. These cannot be exact relative frequencies of student counts.

issues.what: The data series for Class A and Class B are swapped in the drawing parameters compared to the alt text description.
issues.why: In the parameters, 'Class A (40 students)' is assigned the first row of data [0.4, 0.08, 0.12, 0.4] and 'Class B (25 students)' is assigned the second row [0.2, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4]. However, the alt text states that Class A has 20% walk, 10% bike, 30% bus, 40% car (which is the second row) and Class B has 40% walk, 8% bike, 12% bus, 40% car (which is the first row). This swap causes the chart's visual representation to contradict its description.

issues.what: The title, subtitle, note, and alt text claim that the result distributions differ and indicate association.
issues.why: Both groups have the same distribution: 35/50 = 28/40 = 70% pass, and 15/50 = 12/40 = 30% do not pass. These data show no association between part-time job status and exam result.

issues.what: The title, subtitle, and alt text claim that the distributions differ and are associated, but the actual data shows they are identical.
issues.why: For the 'Has a part-time job' group, the pass rate is 35/50 = 70%. For the 'No part-time job' group, the pass rate is 28/40 = 70%. Since both groups have an identical 70% pass rate, the distributions do not differ, meaning there is no association between the two variables in these data. The figure's text directly contradicts the mathematical reality of the provided data.

issues.what: The alt text and note claim that having a part-time job causes a lower pass rate or exam failure.
issues.why: The counts show different pass rates—30/50 = 60% for students with a job and 32/40 = 80% for students without one—but this establishes association in these data, not causation.

issues.what: The alt text and note assert a causal relationship based on association ("the part-time job causes the lower pass rate", "shows that the job causes them to fail").
issues.why: In statistics, association does not imply causation. Since this is an observational study (students are not randomly assigned to have a part-time job), it is incorrect to claim that the job causes the lower pass rate, as confounding variables may be present. This teaches students a fundamental statistical error.
